newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Norilsk cannot meet wage demands.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Norilsk cannot meet wage demands.

text.p: Russia's giant Norilsk Nickel metals group said on Monday it could not meet union demands for repayment of salary and holiday arrears, hours after union leaders approved a plan to strike later this month.

Group spokesman Sergei Vetchinin said that management at Norilsk, one of the world's most important producers of nickel, cobalt and platinum group metals, could pay off the arrears over the course of this year.
But a labour representative at Norilsk's flagship Arctic plant, where workers have threated to strike, said earlier that this was too long.
The United Trade Union committee, the main union at the flagship Norilsk mining and metallurgical combine, said it would call a strike if demands were not met within 10 days.
"The period which the trade union is demanding for repayment is objectively impossible," Vetchinin said.

The Norilsk Nickel group, called RAO Norilsky Nickel in Russian, accounts for nearly 20 percent of annual world nickel supply and 60 percent of palladium supplies. Prices of nickel, platinum and palladium have risen in recent weeks on concerns over Norilsk supplies.

The comments by Vetchinin, who speaks for management, and by the union followed a March 1 meeting of labour and management representatives in the inhospitable town of Norilsk, 320 km (200 miles) north of the Arctic Circle.
RAO Norilsky Nickel said on Friday that it viewed any labour strike at the main plant as a move that could scupper a repayment schedule, since full production was the only way of raising money.

Vetchinin said the only way payments to workers could be accelerated was by shifting some of the enormous social costs shouldered by the company to the regional Krasnoyarsk budget. Norilsk says it spent 42 percent of its 1996 revenue on supporting social infrastructure at its company towns.
Vetchinin said company officials were meeting local authorities to ask them to pay for things such as roads and telecommunications in the production towns.

Boris Degtyaryov, deputy head of the union committee, said on Monday that the timing of any strike and the number of workers involved still had to be decided by a committee coordinating talks with management.

But he said at least 50,000 workers involved in production and processing of non-ferrous and precious metals could lay down their tools. The maximum number of workers involved would be 120,000 -- the plant's entire workforce.

Norilsk's main shareholder, commercial bank Uneximbank, is struggling to implement a rescue package for the Soviet-era metals monolith, which was a showpiece of the Communist planned economy and Moscow's drive to tap metals reserves at any cost.
Degtyaryov said it was not too late to resolve the dispute, adding that the committee should do everything to continue a dialogue with management.
"A perfect outcome would be that if all our legitimate demands were met. There would be no strike," he said.
Russia feeds 25 to 30 percent of western European nickel demand. Stainless steel is the main end-use for nickel, and accounts for around two thirds of nickel consumption.
The Norilsk group owes workers 900 billion roubles ($160 million) in salary and holiday arrears and 1.2 trillion roubles ($211 million) to various budgets.
Workers at the plant have also demanded wages be increased by what RAO Norilsky Nickel has said would cost the company 70 billion roubles a month.
The main metals plant last year produced 100,000 tonnes of nickel from the group's total output of 177,185 tonnes. Total world production is around one million tonnes a year.
--Moscow Newsroom +7095 941 8520 ($1=5,678 roubles)
